newsitem.title: USA: Jobless rate edges up to 5.4 percent in January.
newsitem.headline: Jobless rate edges up to 5.4 percent in January.

text.p: The unemployment rate edged up to 5.4 percent last month from 5.3 percent in December, even though the economy created more jobs than it has since last summer, the government said on Friday.

In the government's first reading of the nation's economic health in January, the Labour Department reported that 271,000 non-farm jobs were created, the most since August, after payrolls grew by 261,000 jobs in December.
Economists surveyed by Reuters had expected a jobless rate of 5.2 percent and payroll growth of 237,000 in January.

Traders in the financial markets, attuned to hints of stronger inflation, had anxiously awaited the report for signs of whether the job market was tightening enough for employers to bid up wages, which could prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.

In the inflation-sensitive bond market, the bellwether 30-year U.S. Treasury bond gained a full point and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, fell to 6.68 percent from 6.76 percent Thursday.

"Hourly earnings were much less than expected and the unemployment rate rose. It is fairly benign and the rally in bonds is a sigh of relief that the data were not worse," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities.

The Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee this week left rates unchanged, at least until its next meeting in March. But at its Dec. 17 meeting it agreed that rates were more likely to rise than fall in the future.

With the economy about to complete its sixth year of uninterrupted growth and the jobless rate at less than 6 percent for well over two years, economists have said some pickup in inflation is likely eventually.

But average hourly wages rose only 1 cent last month to $12.06, after gaining 15 cents in the previous two months, the department said. Over the past 12 months they rose by 3.8 percent, slightly faster than 3.3 percent rise in consumer prices in 1996.
The department's more comprehensive Employment Cost Index, however, rose only 2.9 percent in 1996.
The slight rise in the January jobless rate to 5.4 percent was statistically insignificant, according to Katharine Abraham, commissioner of the department's Bureau of Labour Statistics.

The department's household survey last month showed a rise of 75,000 unemployed workers to 7.27 million and a gain of 433,000 jobholders to 128.58 million. The growth of the civilian labour force, which includes all those working or looking for jobs, reflects a revision in the population estimate used by the department.
The department's survey of businesses showed strong job gains in a temporary services and health care in January, but slower growth in retail and in business service jobs.

The number of manufacturing jobs last month grew by 18,000 after adding 14,000 jobs in December, the department said. Factory overtime hours were unchanged at 4.6 hours per week, while the factory work week fell by 18 minutes to 41.7 hours, largely because of bad weather, it said.
Nasty weather also accounted for slower growth in construction jobs. The industry added 14,000 jobs last month after a 55,000 gain in the previous two months, the department said.
Because of a number of statistical quirks, the number of jobs in specific industries last month may be overstated or understated, Abraham said.

"The net effect of all these special factors on aggregate payroll employment growth was small, although estimates for specific industries may be somewhat over- or understated," she said in prepared testimony for the congressional Joint Economic Committee.
For all of 1996, a total of 2.6 million new jobs were generated, compared with an increase of 2.2 million in 1995.
